scenarios.title: Scenario 3 — Multi-Agent Research System
scenarios.domains: D1 Agentic Architecture · D2 Tool Design & MCP · D5 Context & Reliability
scenarios.brief: A market-intelligence firm runs a research system on the Claude Agent SDK. A coordinator agent delegates through the Task tool to web-search, document-analysis, synthesis and report-generation subagents, each running in its own context. The document-analysis subagent reads the firm's internal research library over MCP. Analysts receive cited reports of about 4,000 words, and a full run takes 8–14 minutes.

scenarios.title: Scenario 4 — Developer Productivity with Claude
scenarios.domains: D2 Tool Design & MCP · D1 Agentic Architecture · D3 Claude Code Configuration
scenarios.brief: An engineer has joined the team that owns a 400,000-line Python and TypeScript service. They work in Claude Code with the built-in tools (Read, Write, Edit, Bash, Grep, Glob) and MCP servers for GitHub and Jira. The same repository holds the Terraform that manages production. Shared configuration should arrive with a clone; personal setups stay personal.

questions.question: An analyst asked how supply constraints are affecting electric-vehicle makers' 2027 production plans. The report covered lithium, cobalt and nickel pricing in depth and said almost nothing about cell-manufacturing capacity, which the analyst regards as the binding constraint. None of its 61 citations is to a battery-cell producer. Each search subagent was briefed on one of the three metals and returned more than 30 relevant sources. Before synthesis, the coordinator's review step checked the findings against its three subtasks and marked coverage complete. What is the most likely root cause?

options.t: The web-search subagents' queries had too little recall to reach battery-cell producers' filings and the trade press that covers them.
options.why: Runner-up. Weak search recall would be the cause if a subagent had been briefed on cell capacity and still came back empty. Each one was briefed on a single metal and found plenty, so search did its assigned job.

options.t: The document-analysis subagent set aside cell-capacity material as outside the metals focus that its own brief had described.
options.why: Incorrect. Filtering in analysis would show up as cell-capacity sources retrieved and then dropped. No search was ever asked to look for them, so there was nothing to drop.

options.t: The coordinator framed the request as a raw-materials question, and its review step judged completeness against that same framing.
options.why: Correct. The decomposition left out a whole area of the question, and the review compared findings with the coordinator's own plan rather than with the analyst's request, so the gap certified itself.

options.t: The synthesis subagent left out manufacturing-capacity claims that lacked support from at least two independent sources.
options.why: Incorrect. Synthesis can only drop claims it received. With no subtask covering cell capacity, there were no such claims to weigh.

questions.decider: Each search subagent was briefed on one metal and returned plenty, and the review checked against the coordinator's own three subtasks; if a subagent had been asked about cell capacity and come back empty, weak search recall would be the cause.
questions.explanation: Overly narrow decomposition leaves whole areas of a broad question uncovered, and subagents that succeed within their assigned scope are no evidence against it. A coverage check only helps if it measures against the original request, not against the coordinator's plan.

eli5.question: A report missed the most important part of the topic. The question asks why. The clue is: each search helper was briefed on one of the three metals, and the review checked the findings against those same three subtasks. 'No citations to cell producers' tempts you to blame search; it is a result, not the cause.
eli5.answer: Picture a teacher who splits a class project into three chapters and then marks it complete because all three chapters were handed in. Nobody checked the project against the actual assignment. Here the coordinator split the question too narrowly (task decomposition), and its review compared the work with its own plan, not with the analyst's question. Each helper did its job perfectly inside a box that was too small. Rule: when every helper succeeds and the answer is still incomplete, look at how the work was split.
options: Runner-up. Weak searches (low recall) would explain this if a helper had been asked about cell capacity and found nothing. No helper was asked.
The reading helper (document analysis) can only throw away what it receives. Nothing about cell capacity was ever fetched.
Correct. The split left out a whole area, and the review checked the split against itself.
The writing helper (synthesis) can only drop claims it was given. No cell-capacity claims ever reached it.

deep.premise: You'd think a missing topic means a search problem, because the visible symptom is missing sources. But searches only look where they are sent. When every subagent finishes well and the gap is a whole area, the fault is upstream: the coordinator's split of the question. And a review that checks the work against that same split cannot catch it, because it is marking the plan against itself.

questions.question: Over several turns the coordinator retrieves three supplier contracts and agrees with the analyst which industry pricing benchmark to use. It then spawns the document-analysis subagent with the Task prompt: 'Compare the pricing terms in the contracts we reviewed against the agreed benchmark.' The subagent returns a careful, well-formatted comparison of two other contracts from the library against a 2023 benchmark. Analysts choose the benchmark afresh for each engagement, and the contracts differ every time. Which change fixes this?

options.t: Restate the Task prompt as the goal of the comparison and the quality bar it must meet, leaving the method for the subagent to choose.
options.why: Incorrect. Goals and quality criteria beat step-by-step procedures in a delegation prompt, but this prompt is already short and goal-shaped. What it lacks is the material, not a better framing.

options.t: Add the benchmark and the comparison method to the document-analysis subagent's AgentDefinition as standing system-prompt instructions.
options.why: Runner-up. Standing instructions in the AgentDefinition fit facts that hold on every run. The benchmark and the contracts change with each engagement, so they have to travel in the prompt for this run.

options.t: Have the subagent return each comparison with contract name, clause and page held in fields separate from the comparison text.
options.why: Incorrect. Separating content from source metadata protects attribution. It does nothing about a subagent that never received the right contracts or benchmark.

options.t: Put the full text of the three contracts, the coordinator's findings so far and the chosen benchmark into the Task prompt itself.
options.why: Correct. A subagent starts with an isolated context and inherits nothing from the coordinator's conversation. Everything it needs for this run must be written into its prompt.

questions.decider: The benchmark and the contracts change with every engagement; if they were the same on every run, standing instructions in the AgentDefinition would be a reasonable home for them.
questions.explanation: Subagents run in isolated context and do not see the coordinator's history. Anything specific to this run, including prior findings, must be passed explicitly and completely in the spawn prompt; standing instructions suit only what never changes.

eli5.question: A helper compared the wrong contracts against the wrong benchmark. The question asks how to fix that. The clue is: the benchmark and the contracts change with every engagement. The neat, well-formatted output is a distraction; the helper simply never got the material.
eli5.answer: Imagine sending a courier to 'deliver the parcel we talked about' when the courier was never in the room. They will grab some parcel and deliver it beautifully to the wrong place. A helper agent is that courier: it starts with an empty memory (isolated context) and sees only its instructions. So the contracts, the earlier findings and the chosen benchmark must go into this run's instructions (the Task prompt). Rule: a subagent knows only what you write in its prompt.
options: Writing the goal and quality bar (goal-based prompts) is good style. But the helper still won't have the contracts or the benchmark.
Runner-up. Standing instructions (the AgentDefinition system prompt) suit facts that never change. Here the benchmark and contracts change every time.
Keeping source details in separate fields (structured metadata) protects citations. It doesn't give the helper the right material.
Correct. Put the contracts, earlier findings and chosen benchmark into this run's prompt.

deep.premise: It is tempting to think a subagent picks up the conversation it was spawned from, so a prompt like 'the contracts we reviewed' makes sense. It doesn't. A subagent starts with isolated context: no history, no shared memory. The other trap is the right fix in the wrong home: standing instructions are for what is true on every run, and this benchmark is not.

questions.question: Every report the firm sells has four mandatory evidence sections: competitor filings, academic literature, news coverage and regulatory notices, each gathered by its own search subagent. The coordinator writes all four search briefs from the analyst's question before any search starts. It then issues one delegation, waits for the result, and issues the next. Each search takes 2–3 minutes, the sources they fetch overlap by under 3%, and a 12-minute wait is the top complaint in analyst feedback. Which change most reduces wall-clock time?

options.t: Have the coordinator send narrow questions down a shorter path that skips the search sections those questions do not need.
options.why: Runner-up. Choosing subagents by query complexity is the right fix when many requests do not need every stage. Here all four sections are mandatory in every report, so nothing can be skipped.

options.t: Have the coordinator emit all four search delegations within a single response and gather the results as each one returns.
options.why: Correct. The four briefs are written before any search runs, so none depends on another. Multiple Task calls in one response run the searches concurrently, and the phase costs about the slowest search instead of the sum.

options.t: Partition the four search scopes more tightly and remove the topics that more than one search subagent currently covers.
options.why: Incorrect. Partitioning scope to avoid duplicate work is good practice, but the overlap is already under 3%. There is little time to win there.

options.t: Pass each search subagent a structured brief holding the analyst's question, the coordinator's plan and the other three scopes.
options.why: Incorrect. Complete, structured context in a delegation prompt is good practice, but it does not change the fact that the four searches run one after another.

questions.decider: All four sections are mandatory and all four briefs exist before any search starts; if many requests needed only some sections, selecting subagents by query complexity would save more.
questions.explanation: Independent subtasks should run concurrently: the coordinator spawns parallel subagents by emitting several Task calls in one response. Sequential delegation is for genuine dependencies, and dynamic subagent selection is for requests that do not need every stage.

eli5.question: Reports take too long. The question asks what saves the most time. The clue is: the coordinator writes all four search briefs before any search starts, and all four sections are mandatory. So the searches don't need each other and none can be skipped.
eli5.answer: Think of four errands that don't depend on each other. Sending one friend, waiting for them to come back, then sending the next, takes four times as long as sending all four friends at once. The coordinator can do that by putting all four delegations in one reply (multiple Task calls in one response), and they run at the same time. The wait drops to about the slowest search. Rule: if jobs don't depend on each other, start them together.
options: Runner-up. Skipping unneeded helpers (dynamic subagent selection) saves time when some questions need fewer sections. Here every section is mandatory.
Correct. Send all four delegations in one reply so the searches run in parallel.
Cutting overlap (scope partitioning) helps when helpers repeat each other. Overlap is already under 3%.
Richer briefs (explicit context) make each helper better, but they still run one after another.

deep.premise: You'd think the way to make a pipeline faster is to do less: skip steps, trim scope. Sometimes it is. But when every step is required, the win is in doing independent steps at the same time. The Agent SDK runs Task calls in parallel when the coordinator emits several in one response.

questions.question: While formatting a report, the report-generation subagent pauses to confirm details about the companies it mentions. Logs from 400 runs show 82% of these checks are one-field lookups, such as a legal entity name or an exchange ticker; the rest ask whether a subsidiary's revenue is already counted in its parent's figure, which means reconciling several filings. About 60% of the companies checked first appear inside quoted source passages rather than in the coordinator's outline. Each check travels through the coordinator and adds roughly 25 seconds. Which change best fits?

options.t: Give the report subagent a narrow company-lookup tool for single-field checks; consolidation questions still go to the coordinator.
options.why: Correct. A limited cross-role tool removes the round trip for the frequent, simple case, while the rarer reconciliation work stays with the coordinator, which can delegate it properly.

options.t: Have the coordinator look up names and tickers for the companies it expects to appear and pass them as a table in the subagent's prompt.
options.why: Runner-up. Passing needed facts explicitly in the prompt is good practice and would win if the companies were known in advance. Most of them first appear in quoted passages, so a table built from the outline misses them.

options.t: Give the report subagent the web-search subagent's full toolset and let it settle any company question while it drafts.
options.why: Incorrect. Off-specialisation tools tend to be misused, and reconciling subsidiaries is research the coordinator should own. A narrow tool covers the common case without that risk.

options.t: Have the report subagent mark each unresolved company detail and send the coordinator one batch of checks after drafting.
options.why: Incorrect. Batching cuts round trips but leaves formatting blocked on unresolved details, and the coordinator still handles 82% of checks that need no coordination.

questions.decider: Most companies first appear inside quoted passages, so they cannot be resolved from the outline in advance; if the companies were all known up front, a prefetched table in the prompt would do the job without a new tool.
questions.explanation: Scope each agent's tools to its role, then make a deliberate exception for a high-frequency, simple need: a narrow cross-role tool. Keep work that needs coordination flowing through the coordinator.

eli5.question: The report helper keeps asking the boss small questions, and each one costs 25 seconds. The question asks for the best fix. The clue is: most of the companies it checks first appear inside quoted passages, not in the coordinator's outline. So nobody can look them up in advance.
eli5.answer: Picture a writer who walks to the editor's office every time they need a company's ticker symbol. Give the writer a small phone book for simple lookups, and keep sending the hard questions to the editor. In agent terms that phone book is a narrow cross-role tool: limited, for one frequent, simple need. Complex reconciliation still goes through the coordinator, which can delegate it properly. Rule: give a helper a small tool for its frequent simple need; keep the hard cases with the coordinator.
options: Correct. A small lookup tool for one-field checks; the hard reconciliation questions still go to the coordinator.
Runner-up. Handing over a ready-made table (explicit context) works when you know the companies in advance. Most appear only in quoted passages.
Giving the writer every research tool (over-provisioning) invites misuse, and reconciliation is research the coordinator should own.
Saving questions for one batch at the end (batching) leaves formatting stuck, and the coordinator still handles all the simple checks.

deep.premise: You'd think the clean answer is either 'route everything through the coordinator' or 'pre-load everything the subagent might need'. Both are good habits. But pre-loading only works when you can predict the need, and routing everything wastes time on trivial lookups. The guide's middle path is a scoped cross-role tool for the high-frequency simple case.

questions.question: A client found that a report attributed a 14% churn figure to an industry survey that never mentions churn, and a spot check then found about one claim in eleven cited to the wrong source. Document-analysis summaries hold separate fields for document name, page and URL. The synthesis subagent reads those summaries and writes continuous prose; the report generator then attaches a citation to each sentence by finding the summary it most resembles. Which change addresses the root cause?

options.t: Add an independent reviewer instance that checks each cited claim against its source before the report is released.
options.why: Runner-up. An independent reviewer is the right tool when you need to catch errors before release. It would win if the question asked how to stop bad citations reaching clients this week; it leaves the pipeline still guessing citations.

options.t: Make document analysis return its summaries with content and source metadata held in separate structured fields.
options.why: Incorrect. That separation is good practice, and the summaries already have it. The link between claim and source is lost later, when synthesis turns them into prose.

options.t: Raise the report generator's similarity threshold and leave a sentence uncited when no summary matches it closely.
options.why: Incorrect. A stricter threshold trades wrong citations for missing ones. Matching after the fact is still inference, not the record of where a claim came from.

options.t: Have synthesis emit each claim with the IDs of the summaries it used, and build the citations from those links.
options.why: Correct. Attribution is lost when synthesis compresses without keeping claim-to-source mappings. Carrying the mapping through synthesis removes the guesswork at its source.

questions.decider: Citations are rebuilt by resemblance after synthesis has already discarded the claim-to-source link, and the question asks for the root cause; if it asked for the fastest way to stop bad citations reaching clients, an independent review pass would win.
questions.explanation: Source attribution is lost when summarisation or synthesis compresses content without preserving claim-source mappings. Preserve the mapping structurally through every stage instead of reconstructing it downstream.

eli5.question: Citations point to the wrong sources. The question asks for the root cause. The clue is: citations are added after the prose is written, by finding the summary each sentence most resembles. The angry client and the churn figure are the vivid part; they tempt you toward a checker.
eli5.answer: Imagine writing an essay from twenty sets of notes, then afterwards guessing which notes each sentence came from by how similar they look. You will guess wrong sometimes. The fix is to write the source next to each claim as you write it. In the pipeline, synthesis should output each claim with links to the summaries it used (claim-source mappings), and citations are built from those links. Rule: carry the source with the claim; never rebuild it afterwards.
options: Runner-up. A second checker (independent review) catches bad citations before release. It would win if the question asked for a quick safety net, but the pipeline would still be guessing.
Keeping source details in separate fields (structured metadata) is good, and the summaries already do it. The link is lost later, at synthesis.
A stricter similarity score swaps wrong citations for missing ones. It is still guessing.
Correct. Synthesis records which summaries each claim came from, and citations use those links.

deep.premise: You'd think wrong citations need a better checker. A checker catches mistakes; it doesn't stop them being made. The mistakes come from a design that throws away the claim-to-source link during synthesis and then tries to guess it back by similarity. The root fix is to keep the link the whole way.

questions.question: In a cloud-security market report, the synthesis subagent stated the market size as $7.1B. Two other reputable sources gathered in the same run gave $4.2B and $4.6B, and analysts only learned of them by reading raw subagent output. The document-analysis summaries record each figure and the source it came from, but nothing about when it was measured. The research director's rule is that analysts, not the system, settle disputed numbers, and the report must give them enough to do it. Which TWO changes best meet this rule?

options.t: When figures disagree, have the coordinator commission a targeted search for a third independent source before synthesis continues.
options.why: Runner-up. Re-delegating to fill a gap is sound practice, and more evidence can help. But it does not show analysts the disagreement or tell them how the figures differ; the system would still be the one presenting a settled answer.

options.t: Report every disagreeing figure side by side with its source attribution and an explicit note that the sources conflict.
options.why: Correct. Annotating conflicting statistics with their sources, instead of picking one, puts the dispute in front of the analyst who is meant to settle it.

options.t: Rank sources by publisher reputation and report the top-ranked figure, listing the others in a footnote.
options.why: Incorrect. This is still the system choosing, and reputation is a weak proxy: here all three sources are reputable.

options.t: Have the synthesis subagent attach a numeric confidence score to each figure it reports.
options.why: Incorrect. Self-reported confidence is poorly calibrated, and a score on one number does not show the analyst the competing figures.

options.t: Require each extracted statistic to carry its publication or collection date from analysis through to the report.
options.why: Correct. Without dates, a 2022 survey and a 2025 estimate look like a contradiction. Dates let analysts tell real disagreement from figures measured at different times.

questions.decider: The director wants analysts to settle disputes and the summaries carry no measurement dates; if the goal were for the system itself to resolve the dispute more reliably, a targeted search for more evidence would be one of the two.
questions.explanation: Annotate conflicting statistics with source attribution instead of picking one, and carry publication or collection dates so temporal differences are not misread as contradictions. Both preserve what a reader needs to judge for themselves.

eli5.question: Sources disagree about a market's size, and the system quietly picked one. The question asks which two changes let analysts settle disputes themselves. The clue is: the summaries record nothing about when each figure was measured. A disagreement might really be two different years.
eli5.answer: Think of a referee's job versus a reporter's. The director wants the system to report, not referee. So the report should show every disagreeing figure with where it came from (attribution), and each figure should carry its date (publication or collection date). With both, an analyst can see the dispute and tell a real disagreement from 'this one is from 2022'. Rule: when sources disagree, show both with sources and dates; don't pick one.
options: Runner-up. Hunting for a third source (re-delegation) is sound research, but the system would still be the one deciding. Analysts still wouldn't see the dispute or the dates.
Correct. Show every disagreeing figure side by side with its source, and say they conflict.
Ranking by reputation is still the system choosing, and all three sources are reputable.
A self-reported confidence number (self-rated confidence) is poorly calibrated and hides the competing figures.
Correct. Carry each figure's date so analysts can spot figures from different years.

deep.premise: You'd think the system's job is to find the right number, so more evidence or a smarter tie-break must help. Here the director has said the opposite: analysts settle disputes. Then the system's job is to show the dispute and give the context needed to judge it, and the most common hidden context is time.

questions.question: The document-analysis subagent is assigned fifteen documents from the internal library. It analyses seven; every request for the remaining eight returns the MCP error 'access denied: collection restricted to the M&A desk'. Today the subagent retries each one four times with backoff, which takes about six minutes, then returns 'analysis failed' as its entire output, and the coordinator stops the run. Other collections hold related but less specific material. What should the subagent do instead?

options.t: Keep the backoff retries for the eight documents, then pass the coordinator their identifiers along with the seven finished analyses.
options.why: Runner-up. Local retry before propagating is right for transient faults such as timeouts, and passing partial results up is right too. A permission denial will not clear on retry, so the six minutes are wasted and the error's nature is not reported.

options.t: Replace the eight documents with the closest matches from open collections and complete the analysis without raising an error.
options.why: Incorrect. Quietly substituting weaker material suppresses the failure. The coordinator and the analyst never learn that the report rests on less specific sources.

options.t: Stop retrying; return the seven analyses plus a structured error naming the category, the eight documents and open alternatives.
options.why: Correct. Structured error context (failure type, what was attempted, partial results, alternatives) lets the coordinator choose: proceed with partial coverage, re-scope, or ask the analyst.

options.t: Escalate each denial to the analyst as it occurs and hold the run until access to the restricted collection is granted.
options.why: Incorrect. Human escalation has its place, but pausing on each denial skips the coordinator, which owns recovery and may well proceed with partial coverage.

questions.decider: The error is a permission denial, which retrying cannot fix; if the failures were timeouts, retrying locally before reporting up with partial results would be the better first move.
questions.explanation: Subagents should recover locally where recovery is possible and propagate what they cannot resolve as structured error context with partial results. Generic failure strings, silent suppression and stopping on a single failure all deny the coordinator what it needs to recover.

Better: stop knocking, report the seven delivered, say which eight are stuck and why, and mention a side entrance. That report is structured error context: what failed, why, what was done, and options. Then the boss (the coordinator) decides. Rule: report what failed, why, and what you already have, so the coordinator can choose.
options: Runner-up. Retrying first (local recovery) is right for temporary faults like timeouts. A permission denial won't clear, so the retries waste six minutes.
Quietly swapping in weaker documents (silent suppression) hides the failure from everyone.
Correct. Stop retrying; send back the seven results with a clear, labelled error and alternatives.
Pausing for a human on every denial skips the coordinator, which may be happy to go on with partial coverage.

deep.premise: You'd think retry-then-report is always the mature pattern. It is, for transient errors such as timeouts. A permission error is not transient: no amount of backoff opens a restricted collection. The skill is to classify the error, stop retrying when retry can't help, and pass up structured context with partial results.

questions.question: Every request runs the same chain: search, document analysis, synthesis, then a 4,000-word report. About a third of requests are single-fact questions, such as a competitor's most recent funding round, which analysts usually ask while on a call with a client. Those runs still take 9–12 minutes and cost about $3 each, and finance has flagged the monthly bill. Broad landscape questions, the other two-thirds, are well served by the full chain. Which change best addresses this?

options.t: Let the coordinator choose subagents per request, giving single-fact questions a search and a short answer.
options.why: Correct. The coordinator should select subagents by query complexity. Single-fact questions get a fast, cheap path; landscape questions keep the full pipeline.

options.t: Send the single-fact questions through the Message Batches API and keep the full chain in real time for landscape work.
options.why: Runner-up. Batch processing halves cost and suits work nobody is waiting for. These questions are asked live on client calls, and batch results can take up to 24 hours.

options.t: Have the coordinator emit the four stage delegations as parallel Task calls instead of waiting for each stage to finish.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel spawning suits independent work. Each stage here consumes the previous stage's output, and running them together would not make a single-fact run need fewer stages.

options.t: Cap each run's iterations at a fixed count and return the best answer the pipeline has produced when the cap is hit.
options.why: Incorrect. An arbitrary cap is a weak stopping rule; it truncates landscape reports as well, and single-fact runs would still pass through every stage.

questions.decider: Single-fact questions are asked while analysts are on a client call; if they could wait until the next day, sending them through the Message Batches API would cut cost with less design change.
questions.explanation: A fixed pipeline suits work whose shape is known in advance. When incoming requests vary in complexity, the coordinator should choose which subagents to invoke per request rather than route everything through the full chain.

eli5.question: Simple questions go through the whole expensive pipeline. The question asks for the best fix. The clue is: analysts ask these questions while on a call with a client. Finance's bill is the vivid part, and it tempts you toward the cheapest option.
eli5.answer: Picture a restaurant that cooks a five-course meal every time someone asks for a glass of water. The head waiter should decide per order what the kitchen needs to do. Here the coordinator should pick which helpers each request needs (dynamic subagent selection): a single fact gets a search and a short answer, a broad question gets the full chain. That cuts both the bill and the wait. Rule: match the pipeline to the question; don't run every request through every stage.
options: Correct. The coordinator picks helpers per request, so single facts take a short path.
Runner-up. The overnight queue (Message Batches API) halves cost, but results can take up to 24 hours. These questions are asked live on calls.
Running stages together (parallel Task calls) needs independent work. Each stage here needs the previous one's output.
A fixed step limit (iteration cap) is a crude stop and would cut the big reports short too.

deep.premise: You'd think a cost complaint calls for a cost tool, and the Batches API is the textbook 50% saving. But batch has no latency promise (up to 24 hours), so it only fits work nobody is waiting for. The real waste is that a single-fact question runs a four-stage pipeline. Fixing that cuts cost and wait together.

questions.question: Each run, the document-analysis subagent spends its first 12–18 MCP calls on the firm's research library, listing folders and opening sample files to learn what each collection holds and how its metadata fields are named, before it analyses anything. The librarians add or reorganise collections most weeks. These exploratory results also crowd the subagent's context, and analysis quality drops on large assignments. Which change best removes this overhead?

options.t: Spawn a separate exploration subagent at the start of each run that maps the library and returns a short summary of it.
options.why: Incorrect. Delegating discovery isolates its verbose output, which helps the context problem, but the same 12–18 calls still happen on every run.

options.t: Publish the library's collection list, folder hierarchy and field definitions on its MCP server as readable resources.
options.why: Correct. MCP resources expose content catalogues such as document hierarchies and schemas, so the agent can read what exists instead of discovering it through exploratory tool calls, and the server keeps them current.

options.t: Write the library's collection taxonomy and metadata field names into the document-analysis subagent's system prompt.
options.why: Runner-up. A static description in the system prompt would remove the exploration if the library rarely changed. Collections change most weeks, so a hand-written taxonomy goes stale.

options.t: Add a search_catalogue tool that takes keywords and returns the matching collections with their metadata field names.
options.why: Incorrect. A keyword search still makes the agent guess what to ask for, one call at a time. The need is to see what exists, which is catalogue content, not an action.

questions.decider: Collections change most weeks, so a hand-written taxonomy would go stale; if the library were stable, writing its structure into the system prompt would remove the exploration just as well.
questions.explanation: MCP tools perform actions; MCP resources expose content the agent can read. Catalogues, document hierarchies and schemas belong in resources, which is how you cut exploratory tool calls while keeping the content current.

In MCP, that catalogue is a resource: content the agent can read directly, as opposed to a tool, which is an action it must call. The server keeps it current as collections change. Rule: things to read go in resources; things to do go in tools.
options: Sending a scout ahead (exploration subagent) keeps the mess out of the main context, but the same calls still happen every run.

A keyword search tool still makes the agent guess what to ask for. It needs to see what exists.

questions.question: After an 11-minute gathering phase, a session holds the full text of 40 retrieved filings and earnings-call transcripts. A client wants two scenario analyses from it: one assuming a 2027 tariff increase, one assuming none. Each analysis must be able to quote any passage of the gathered material, and neither should be influenced by the other's reasoning. The gathering phase is billed to the client and should run once. Which session strategy fits best?

options.t: Write a structured summary of the gathered material and start two new sessions from it, one for each tariff assumption.
options.why: Runner-up. A fresh session seeded with a structured summary is the safer choice when tool results are stale or context is crowded. Here the analyses must quote any passage, and a summary keeps only what it chose to keep.

options.t: Resume the session for the tariff-increase analysis, then resume it again afterwards for the no-increase analysis.
options.why: Incorrect. Resuming continues one line of conversation, so the second analysis would sit on top of the first one's reasoning.

options.t: Ask for both analyses in a single request in the existing session, with a separate heading for each tariff assumption.
options.why: Incorrect. One response written in one context lets each analysis shape the other, which the client ruled out.

options.t: Branch the session twice from its state after gathering, and continue each branch under one of the tariff assumptions.
options.why: Correct. Forking (fork_session) creates independent branches from a shared baseline: both keep every gathered document, neither sees the other's reasoning, and gathering runs once.

questions.decider: Each analysis must be able to quote any passage of the gathered material; if they needed only the main findings, two fresh sessions from a structured summary would serve.
questions.explanation: --resume continues a conversation linearly; fork_session creates independent branches from a shared baseline. When you need divergent continuations of the same established state, with the full state intact, fork.

eli5.question: One expensive research session must feed two separate analyses. The question asks how to set up the sessions. The clue is: each analysis must be able to quote any passage of the gathered material. A summary would not keep every passage.
eli5.answer: Think of photocopying a full research folder so two teams each get the complete original. Neither sees the other's notes, and nobody has to redo the research. In sessions that is a fork: two independent branches from the same saved point (fork_session). Each branch keeps everything gathered, and neither is shaped by the other. Rule: two different directions from the same starting point means fork.
options: Runner-up. Starting fresh from a written summary (fresh session with a structured summary) is right when old results are stale or space is tight. A summary can't hold every passage.
Picking up the same session twice (--resume) continues one line, so the second analysis sits on top of the first.
Writing both in one reply lets each shape the other, which the client ruled out.
Correct. Branch twice from the point after gathering; each branch keeps everything.

deep.premise: You'd think any way of reusing the gathered work is fine, so a tidy summary is the safe choice. A summary is safe for continuing one task with fresh context. But it keeps only what it chose to keep. When each branch must quote anything, and the branches must not influence each other, you need full copies of the same state: a fork.

questions.question: Before turning on a strict type checker, the engineer wants a list of every generated protobuf module in the repository so they can be excluded. The code generator names each output file after its proto with a _pb2.py suffix and writes a 'Generated by the protocol buffer compiler' comment at the top. Some generated modules are leftovers from protos deleted years ago and sit in no build target, and an old formatter pass rewrote the opening lines of many Python files. Which approach produces the list most reliably?

options.why: Correct. Glob matches file paths, and every generated module follows the naming rule, including the orphaned ones.

options.t: Use Grep for the protocol-compiler header comment and take every file that contains it as the list.

options.t: Use Grep with a regular expression on _pb2 to find the import lines that name generated modules.
options.why: Incorrect. That finds files that import generated modules, not the modules themselves, and misses orphans nobody imports.

options.t: Read the build configuration that drives the generator and list each output file that it declares.
options.why: Incorrect. The build configuration only knows current targets; the leftovers from deleted protos are in no build target.

questions.decider: The formatter rewrote opening lines, so the header is unreliable while the file-name rule holds for every generated module; if file names were inconsistent and the header intact, Grep would be the right tool.

questions.question: A generated 900-line deployment config holds four stanzas, one per environment, rendered from the same template, so they differ only in where they sit in the file. Each contains timeout = 30, and only the third, staging, must become 60. Claude's Edit call fails with an error saying the old text matches four locations. options.t: Retry the Edit with a longer old_string that takes in enough neighbouring lines to match a single location.
options.why: Runner-up. Widening the match is the usual first response to a non-unique Edit. It fails here because the stanzas come from one template, so any amount of surrounding text is identical in all four.

options.t: Run Edit with replace_all to set every timeout to 60, then edit the other three back to 30 one at a time.
options.why: Incorrect. After the first step, the three stanzas to restore are again identical to each other, so the follow-up edits hit the same non-unique match.

options.t: Read the whole file, change the value inside the third stanza, and Write the complete file back.
options.why: Correct. Edit needs a unique text match. When none exists, the documented fallback is Read plus Write, where position in the file can be used.

options.t: Run sed through Bash with an address range covering the third stanza's line numbers to change the value.
options.why: Incorrect. Bash is restricted to read-only commands here, and editing by line number from the shell bypasses the file tools the session is set up to use.

questions.decider: The stanzas are rendered from one template, so no amount of neighbouring text is unique; if the surrounding lines differed between environments, widening the Edit match would be the simpler fix.
questions.explanation: Edit makes targeted changes identified by a unique text match. When no unique match can exist, fall back to Read plus Write rather than forcing Edit or going around the file tools.

So you open the whole document, change the third one by its position, and save the whole file. In Claude Code that is Read the file, then Write it back. Rule: if Edit can't find a unique match, fall back to Read + Write.

options.why: Incorrect. Sharing an unstable experimental server with everyone pushes Dana's trial onto the whole team, start-up crashes included.

options.t: Commit .mcp.json with the GitHub server reading ${GITHUB_TOKEN}, and have Dana register the trial server in her ~/.claude.json.

options.why: Incorrect. Compacting summarises the old file contents rather than refreshing them, and the session is not short of space.

questions.question: Having read about context isolation, the engineer proposes that Claude spawn a subagent for each edit in a six-step change, 'so every edit gets a clean context'. Each step changes a few lines and builds on the result of the step before it, and the engineer reviews every diff in the main session before approving the next. Reading the relevant code takes about 2,000 lines in total, and the session sits at 20% of its window. What is the best approach?

options.t: Run the six edits as subagents spawned in one response, then review all six diffs together in the main session.
options.why: Incorrect. Parallel spawning suits independent work. Each step builds on the one before, so running them together breaks the order the change depends on.

options.t: Use a subagent for each edit, passing it the earlier edits' results and the relevant CLAUDE.md content in its prompt.
options.why: Runner-up. If you delegate, passing prior results explicitly is exactly right. Delegation pays off when work produces verbose output worth isolating; these steps are small and reviewed in the main session.

options.t: Run /compact in the main session between edits to keep the working context for each edit small.
options.why: Incorrect. Compacting reduces context use, but at 20% of the window there is nothing to reclaim, and each summary risks losing detail the next step needs.

options.t: Make the six edits in the main session one at a time, with the engineer reviewing each diff as they go.
options.why: Correct. Subagents earn their overhead by isolating verbose work or running independent tasks in parallel. Small, dependent, reviewed steps offer neither, so delegation only adds handoff cost.

questions.decider: The steps are small, dependent and reviewed in the main session, and the context is at 20%; if each step produced long, noisy output, delegating with explicit context would pay off.
questions.explanation: Know when not to delegate. Subagents help when verbose output needs isolating or independent work can run in parallel; small sequential edits reviewed in the main session have neither property.

eli5.question: The engineer wants a separate helper for each tiny edit. The question asks for the best approach. The clue is: each step is small, depends on the step before, and is reviewed in the main session, which is only 20% full.
eli5.answer: Think of hiring a separate builder for each of six small screws, each needing the previous screw in place, while you inspect every one yourself. The hand-offs cost more than the work. Helpers (subagents) pay off when a job produces lots of noisy output to keep out of the way, or when independent jobs can run at once. Small, dependent, reviewed steps have neither. Rule: delegate to isolate noise or run in parallel; otherwise do it yourself.
options: Running them at once (parallel subagents) needs independent steps. Each step here needs the one before.
Runner-up. If you do delegate, passing earlier results in (explicit context) is right. It would win if each step made lots of noisy output worth hiding.
Squeezing the session (/compact) has nothing to reclaim at 20%, and may drop details the next step needs.
Correct. Make the six edits in the main session, one at a time, reviewing each.

But isolation has a price: every subagent starts empty and must be told everything in its prompt, and its results must be passed back. That price is worth paying only when it buys something: isolating verbose output or running independent work in parallel.

questions.question: The repository holds application code and, under infra/, the Terraform for production. options.t: Have the team work in plan mode for any session that might touch infra/, approving each proposed change by hand.
options.why: Incorrect. Plan mode controls how work proceeds, not what is allowed; it relies on a person catching every risky change.

options.why: Incorrect. Raw API calls from the shell give up typed tools, descriptions and structured errors, and put tokens and request-building into every session.

options.why: Incorrect. Resources suit read-only catalogues; commenting and moving issues are actions, which need tools.

questions.decider: The team's differences are reachable through Jira's standard API and community servers already cover them; if the workflow lived in a system with no existing integration, building a custom server would be justified.

eli5.answer: Think of needing a ladder. You buy a standard one and add a sticky note saying 'our shelf is the third rung'. You don't forge your own ladder because your shelves are special.
